{{field-1}}"] ["question-332a6eec-904f-5523-bf1a-c62328e3b046" :question/worked-solution "The supremum of a set $A$ is the smallest upper bound of $A.$

If $A$ is a finite set, the supremum of $A$ equals its maximum. 

First, let's write down all the terms of our set by substituting $n=1,2,3,4$ into the expression for the elements of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)^{1+1}\cdot 1 & =1 \\ (-1)^{2+1}\cdot 2 & =-2 \\ (-1)^{3+1}\cdot 3 & =3 \\ (-1)^{4+1}\cdot 4 & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
A=\{1,\,-2,\,3,\,-4\}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}sup(A) & =max\{1,\,-2,\,3,\,-4\}=3.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-332a6eec-904f-5523-bf1a-c62328e3b046" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-383aa34f-a1d1-5f56-a588-24ec2c1c5712" :answer-field/id #uuid "383aa34f-a1d1-5f56-a588-24ec2c1c5712"] ["answer-3dcae1ab-8b52-5672-bb43-dd85e7593b29" :answer/id #uuid "3dcae1ab-8b52-5672-bb43-dd85e7593b29"] ["answer-3dcae1ab-8b52-5672-bb43-dd85e7593b29" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-3dcae1ab-8b52-5672-bb43-dd85e7593b29" :answer/value "3"] ["answer-field-383aa34f-a1d1-5f56-a588-24ec2c1c5712" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-383aa34f-a1d1-5f56-a588-24ec2c1c5712" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-383aa34f-a1d1-5f56-a588-24ec2c1c5712" :answer-field/correct "answer-3dcae1ab-8b52-5672-bb43-dd85e7593b29"] ["answer-field-383aa34f-a1d1-5f56-a588-24ec2c1c5712" :answer-field/choices "answer-3dcae1ab-8b52-5672-bb43-dd85e7593b29"] ["question-332a6eec-904f-5523-bf1a-c62328e3b046" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-383aa34f-a1d1-5f56-a588-24ec2c1c5712"] [17592186162156 :knowledge-point/questions "question-332a6eec-904f-5523-bf1a-c62328e3b046"] ["question-64fea66a-24ac-5ed4-9315-868a66adf40d" :question/id #uuid "64fea66a-24ac-5ed4-9315-868a66adf40d"] ["question-64fea66a-24ac-5ed4-9315-868a66adf40d" :question/math-academy-id "q-253555"] ["question-64fea66a-24ac-5ed4-9315-868a66adf40d" :question/problem "Consider the set $A=[1,\sqrt{5}].$ Complete the following reasoning to identify $sup(A).$

$$

Therefore, {{field-4}}."] ["question-64fea66a-24ac-5ed4-9315-868a66adf40d" :question/worked-solution "The supremum of a set $A$ is the smallest upper bound of $A.$

To find the supremum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

In our case, we have the following:

- Any number in the set $x\ge \sqrt{5}$ is greater than or equal to the elements of $A.$ Thus, the set $[\sqrt{5},\infty )$ contains only upper bounds of $A.$

- Any number in the set $x<\sqrt{5}$ is **not** an upper bound of $A.$ In other words, we can always find an element of $A$ that is greater than $x$ for any $x<\sqrt{5}.$

Therefore, $[\sqrt{5},\infty )$ is the set of upper bounds of $A,$ and

$$
sup(A)=min\,[\sqrt{5},\infty )=\sqrt{5}.
$$

Notice that $\sqrt{5}$ is also the maximum of $A.$

The completed reasoning is given below.

The supremum of $A$ is the $\text{smallest upper bound}$ of $A.$

The set of upper bounds of $A$ is as follows:

$$
\{x\in R\,:\,x\ge \sqrt{5}\}
$$

Therefore, $sup(A)=\sqrt{5}\in A.$"] ["question-64fea66a-24ac-5ed4-9315-868a66adf40d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-419f4350-8ea2-5ca7-9094-f580a6bac952" ["question-7fdea743-d7bb-5faa-abc9-1bdf19e0dbae" :question/math-academy-id "q-253044"] ["question-7fdea743-d7bb-5faa-abc9-1bdf19e0dbae" :question/problem "Consider the set $A=(-\infty ,-1).$ Complete the following reasoning to determine $inf(A)$ and $sup(A).$

The infimum of $A$ is the {{field-1}} of $A,$ and the supremum is the {{field-2}} of $A.$

Since $A$ is {{field-3}}, we have $inf(A)$ {{field-4}}.

Since $A$ is {{field-5}}, we have $sup(A)$ {{field-6}}."] ["question-7fdea743-d7bb-5faa-abc9-1bdf19e0dbae" :question/worked-solution "The infimum of $A$ is the greatest lower bound of $A,$ and the supremum is the smallest upper bound of $A.$

To find the infimum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

Since $A$ is unbounded below, $A$ has no lower bounds, and $inf(A)=-\infty .$

Next, to find the supremum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

In our case, we have the following:

- Any number in the set $x\ge -1$ is greater than or equal to the elements of $A.$ Thus, the set $[-1,\infty )$ contains only upper bounds of $A.$

- Any number in the set $x<-1$ is **not** an upper bound of $A.$ In other words, we can always find an element of $A$ that is greater than $x$ for any $x<-1.$

Therefore, $[-1,\infty )$ is the set of upper bounds of $A,$ and

$$
sup(A)=min[-1,\infty )=-1.
$$

The completed reasoning is given below.

The infimum of a set $A$ is the $\text{greatest lower bound}$ of $A,$ and the supremum is the $\text{smallest upper bound}$ of $A.$

Since $A$ is $\text{unbounded below},$ we have $inf(A)=-\infty .$

Since $A$ is $\text{bounded above},$ we have $sup(A)=-1.$"] ["question-7fdea743-d7bb-5faa-abc9-1bdf19e0dbae" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] For this set, we have that {{field-1}}."] [17592186162526 :question/worked-solution "The infimum of $A$ is the greatest lower bound of $A.$

To find the infimum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

The elements of $A$ are the terms of the sequence ${a}_{n},$ given by

$$
{a}_{n}=n\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi ),\,n\in N=\{1,2,3,4,…\}.
$$

Let's draw some points of our sequence on the real line:

![](images/bc/bcece2e5bdef3c9d939d953fbeb0c5163d9343004cd309f28db37bf9b5b089ef.png)

We see that ${a}_{n}$ is an oscillating, non-convergent sequence. Moreover, $A$ is unbounded below. "answer-d5186c5a-5a30-5325-9bea-58622f595315"] ["question-2472238f-de89-5651-9808-c29025aa1081" :question/id #uuid "2472238f-de89-5651-9808-c29025aa1081"] ["question-2472238f-de89-5651-9808-c29025aa1081" :question/math-academy-id "q-253514"] ["question-2472238f-de89-5651-9808-c29025aa1081" :question/problem "Consider the following set.

$$

$$

For this set, we have {{field-1}}."] ["question-2472238f-de89-5651-9808-c29025aa1081" :question/worked-solution "The supremum of a set $A$ is the smallest upper bound of $A.$

To find the supremum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

The elements of $A$ are all the terms of the sequence ${a}_{n},$ given by

$$
{a}_{n}=5-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{n},\,n\in N=\{1,2,3,4,…\}.
$$

Let's draw some points of our sequence on the real line:

![](images/1e/1ea2ed214496ed38ae605e9ac64bebd781a0d5529561fce44d98cca6839d6fbb.png)

We see that ${a}_{n}$ is increasing and converges to $5.$ 

So, in our case, we have that

- any number in the set $x\ge 5$ is an upper bound of $A,$

- any number in the set $x<5$ is **not** an upper bound of $A.$ In other words, we can always find a sufficiently large $n$ so that $5-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{n}$ is greater than $x$ for any $x<5.$

Therefore, $[5,\infty )$ is the set of upper bounds of $A,$ and 

$$
sup(A)=min[5,\infty )=5.
$$

Notice that $5$ is *not* the maximum of $A$ (the set $A$ has no maximum). Therefore, we conclude that

$$
sup(A)=5\notin A.
$$"] ["question-2472238f-de89-5651-9808-c29025aa1081" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-236e608b-8ac0-548b-a7ea-fa7e8de10892" :answer-field/id #uuid "answer-field-236e608b-8ac0-548b-a7ea-fa7e8de10892"] [17592186162158 :knowledge-point/questions "question-2472238f-de89-5651-9808-c29025aa1081"] [17592186054602 :question/problem "Use the table below to plot the graph of $y=3x-2.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $y$ |  |  |  |  |"] [17592186054602 :question/worked-solution "First, we fill the table. Given a value of $x,$ we can find the corresponding $y$ by substituting $x$ into the formula $y=3x-2.$
Therefore,

- if $x=0$ then $y=3(0)-2=-2,$

- if $x=1$ then $y=3(1)-2=1,$

- if $x=2$ then $y=3(2)-2=4,$ and

- if $x=3$ then $y=3(3)-2=7.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $y$ | $-2$ | $1$ | $4$ | $7$ |

We plot these $(x,y)$ pairs on the $xy$-plane:

![](images/09/09e670353b2114b229769e2bd6b3eb4a9895389b818fc3f4ace6997a3e7efa3f.png)

Finally, connecting the points gives us a straight line. This is the graph of $y=3x-2.$

![](images/d2/d2d8891102ce99020f544bd8d82a5ff0454080474ce4267ef5285db92f5b2ca0.png)"] [17592186054603 :question/problem "Sketch the graph of $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x+3.$"] [17592186054603 :question/worked-solution "We need to find two distinct points that lie on our line. Any two points will do!

It is often easiest to pick one of the points to have an $x$-coordinate of $x=0.$ So, for the first point, we will let the $x$-coordinate be $x=0.$ Then the $y$-coordinate is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{2}x+3 \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(0)+3 \\  & =0+3 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first point is $(0,3).$

For the second point, let's choose $x=4.$ Then the $y$-coordinate is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{2}x+3 \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(4)+3 \\  & =-2+3 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second point is $(4,1).$

Finally, we plot those two points on the $xy$-plane and draw a line through them. This is the graph of $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x+3.$

![](images/36/36689081acaacb24a09826c3927388697e77d92caeca900d053d33d0f99d2b8c.png)"] [17592186054499 :question/problem "Which of the following gives the graph of the straight line below?

I. $y=2x-1$

II. $y=\dfrac{1}{2}x-1$

III. $2x-y=1$

![](images/93/93dc9d447c15e4597549996b1f0b533cf86783b5cc5df032a4c46d4ca8934abc.png)"] [17592186054499 :question/worked-solution "Let's pick two distinct points on the line. For example, we can choose $A$ and $B$ with coordinates $(0,-1)$ and $(2,3)$, respectively.

![](images/a9/a9f18453dedb1763908825301f80ef86307d3a3aceaf678bbe8579a42a0996f5.png)

Now, we substitute the coordinates of both points in our equations. If both points satisfy an equation, then we can conclude that the equation represents the line in the graph. Otherwise, if any point does *not* satisfy the equation, then we can conclude that the equation does *not* represent the line in the graph.

- Equation I: $y=2x-1.$
Substituting the coordinates of $A(0,-1)$ and $B(2,3),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1) & =2(0)-1 \\ -1 & =-1\,✓ \\ (3) & =2(2)-1 \\ 3 & =3\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the graph of the straight line above?

I. $y+3x=6$

II. $\frac{1}{3}y+x=2$

III. $y=-3x+6$"] ["question-9d3bda62-1eef-5cb9-886b-004877c9a204" :question/worked-solution "Let's pick two distinct points on the line. For example, $A$ and $B$ with coordinates $(0,6)$ and $(2,0)$, respectively.

![](images/d6/d6cb6d026c181d79bda5c809729eb070c554c2025a287577df0330d1dd8a03e7.png)

Now, we substitute the coordinates of both points in our equations. If both points satisfy an equation, then we can conclude that the equation represents the line in the graph. Otherwise, if any point does *not* satisfy the equation, then we can conclude that the equation does *not* represent the line in the graph.

- Equation I: $y+3x=6.$
Substituting the coordinates of $A(0,6)$ and $B(2,0)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(6)+3(0) & =6 \\ 6 & =6\,✓ \\ (0)+3(2) & =6 \\ 6 & =6\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $y+3x=6$ is an equation of the line in the graph.

"![](images/71/716836dd3dfc93ac26bf9a960d5edcd04da96907b98c39e926a917b7b8feeeee.png)

Which of the following gives the graph of the straight line above?

I. $y=-2x+\frac{1}{2}$

II. $y=-\frac{1}{2}x+2$

III. $y=\frac{1}{2}x+2$"] ["question-a635937b-674b-54dd-a770-48fe7b870be8" :question/worked-solution "Let's pick two distinct points on the line. For example, $A$ and $B$ with coordinates $(0,2)$ and $(4,0)$, respectively.

![](images/2b/2b9174d86d123228ae24fffeda4d2e4741e4a776f6671f7eff38340a59ba4d40.png)

Now, we substitute the coordinates of both points in our equations. If both points satisfy an equation, then we can conclude that the equation represents the line in the graph. Otherwise, if any point does *not* satisfy the equation, then we can conclude that the equation does *not* represent the line in the graph.

- Equation I: $y=-2x+\frac{1}{2}.$
Substituting the coordinates of $A(0,2)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(2) & =-1(0)+\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 & =\frac{1}{2}\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $y=-2x+\frac{1}{2}$ is *not* equation of the line in the graph.

- Equation II: $y=-\frac{1}{2}x+2.$
Substituting the coordinates of $A(0,2)$ and $B(4,0)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(2) & =-\frac{1}{2}(0)+2 \\ 2 & =2\,✓ \\ (0) & =-\frac{1}{2}(4)+2 \\ 0 & =-2+2 \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,$y=-\frac{1}{2}x+2$ is an equation of the line in the graph.

- Equation III: $y=\frac{1}{2}x+2.$
Substituting the coordinates of $A(0,2)$ and $B(4,0)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(2) & =\frac{1}{2}(0)+2 \\ 2 & =2\,✓ \\ (0) & =\frac{1}{2}(4)+2 \\ 0 & =2+2 \\ 0 & =4\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $y=\frac{1}{2}x+2$ is *not* equation of the line in the graph.

Of the given equations, the only equation that represented the line in the graph was $y=-\frac{1}{2}x+2,$ corresponding to answer choice II. Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""] ["question-a635937b-674b-54dd-a770-48fe7b870be8" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-44f33cfa-5885-5a2f-90fc-d69e3d361204" To check whether a point lies on the line, we substitute the coordinates of the point into the equation and determine whether the resulting statement is true.

- Substituting the point $A(-1,-2)$ results in a true statement:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4x+2 \\ (-2) & =4(-1)+2 \\ -2 & =-2\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $A$ does lie on the line.

- Substituting the point $B(0,1)$ results in a false statement:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4x+2 \\ (1) & =4(0)+2 \\ 1 & =2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $B$ does not lie on the line.

- Substituting the point $C(1,6)$ results in true statement:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4x+2 \\ (6) & =4(1)+2 \\ 6 & =6\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $C$ does lie on the line.

Finally, only points $A$ and $C$ lie on the line."] ["question-acf0d12e-cf58-5db7-b66f-2999c47f2d4e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] $$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}(1-p)^{x-1}p, & x=1,2,3,… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{x-1}(\frac{1}{4}), & x=1,2,3,… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=3) & =f(3) \\  & ={(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}(\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{9}{64}.\end{aligned}

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}(1-p)^{x-1}p, & x=1,2,3,… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $X∼\text{Geom}(\frac{1}{2}),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x-1}(\frac{1}{2}), & x=1,2,3,… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}

$$

Here, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.9),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}(0.1)^{x-1}(0.9), & x=1,2,3… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are infinitely many values of $X$ such that $X>4.$ However, we can simplify the computation by using the complement instead:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>4) & =1-P(X\le 4)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 4) & =P(X\in \{1,2,3,4\}) \\  & =P(X=1)+P(X=2)+P(X=3)+P(X=4) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+f(4) \\  & =(0.1)^{0}(0.9)+(0.1)^{1}(0.9)+(0.1)^{2}(0.9)+(0.1)^{3}(0.9) \\  & =0.9999.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>4) & =1-P(X\le 4) \\  & =1-0.9999 \\  & =0.0001.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-409b1f60-69c1-5499-92f9-7ef6676bbb2d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-1cf79bbd-87e9-5932-996b-d7506f0bd20e" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}(1-p)^{x-1}p, & x=1,2,3,… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $X∼\text{Geom}(\frac{5}{7}),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{(\frac{2}{7})}^{x-1}(\frac{5}{7}), & x=1,2,3… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are infinitely many values of $X$ such that $X\ge 3.$ However, we can simplify the computation by using the complement instead:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 3) & =1-P(X<3)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<3) & =P(X\in \{1,2\}) \\  & =P(X=1)+P(X=2) \\  & =f(1)+f(2) \\  & ={(\frac{2}{7})}^{0}(\frac{5}{7})+{(\frac{2}{7})}^{1}(\frac{5}{7}) \\  & ≈0.9184.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 3) & =1-P(X<3) \\  & ≈1-0.9184 \\  & =0.0816.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-075d366c-d06a-5f72-a1db-49d33772eb88" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-5526fa50-a4a2-58c4-84bf-0839d0ec3ffd" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-075d366c-d06a-5f72-a1db-49d33772eb88"] [17592186168075 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we have a sequence of Bernoulli trials, each resulting in success or failure, and with a probability of success $p.$ Let the random variable $X$ represent the number of Bernoulli trials *until the first success*.

It can be shown that $X$ follows a **geometric distribution** and has the following probability mass function:

![](images/13/13d0eefea25458f7778607118a7673506900d72ee5b8a41826378c8737317e9e.svg)

Let's break this formula down a bit:

- The factor $(1-p)^{x-1}$ represents the probability of getting exactly $(x-1)$ failures, each with probability $(1-p).$

- The factor ${\color{purple}{p}}$ represents the probability of getting a single success.

- The condition $x=1,2,3,\ldots$ indicates that the sequence of Bernoulli trials terminates after a minimum of $1$ trial, and there is no maximum number of trials.

If a random variable $X$ follows a geometric distribution, we say it is a geometric random variable and  write 

$$
X\sim \textrm{Geom}(p).
$$"] [17592186168108 :tutorial/content "You might be wondering where the geometric distribution gets its name. The answer is that the probability mass function forms a geometric sequence! 

Suppose that $X\sim \textrm{Geom}(p).$ Then, the probability mass function for this geometric distribution is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-p)^{x-1}p \\ f(x) & =p(1-p)^{x-1} \\ {{f(x)}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{x}} & ={{p}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}\cdot ({{1-p}_{⏟}}_{r})^{x-1} \\ {a}_{x} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we see that the probability mass function can be interpreted as a geometric sequence where the first term is $a_1=p,$ and the common ratio is $r=1-p.$

Moreover, notice that $f(x)$ satisfies all the criteria to be a probability mass function, namely

1\. $0 \leq f(x) \leq 1$ for all $x$ in $S$

2\. $\displaystyle \sum\limits_{x \in S} f(x) = 1$

Criterion 1 is clearly true because $0 \leq p \leq 1.$ 

To show that criterion 2 is true, we simply need to calculate the sum of this infinite geometric series, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{x\in S}f(x) & ={\sum }_{x=1}^{\infty }p(1-p)^{x-1} \\  & =\frac{p}{1-(1-p)} \\  & =\frac{p}{p} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is indeed a probability distribution."] [17592186167045 :activity/expected-seconds 1140.0] ["question-9d214df3-aafe-5a52-bd67-2c23fbad240f" :question/id #uuid "9d214df3-aafe-5a52-bd67-2c23fbad240f"] ["question-9d214df3-aafe-5a52-bd67-2c23fbad240f" :question/math-academy-id "q-34734"] ["question-9d214df3-aafe-5a52-bd67-2c23fbad240f" :question/problem "![](images/58/582236fbb64c0ebeda310cb0007435d4044295b232499ff5771ede846a1b6d05.png)

The region $D$ is enclosed between the curve ${x}^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=1$ and the line $y=1,$ as shown above. What is
${∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?"] [17592186157834 :question/worked-solution "We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at $(0,1).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y-1)^{2} & =1 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)^{2} & =1 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1 & =1 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

- For $y=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =1 \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ r & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ r & =\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the points $(-1,1)$ and $(1,1).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{4},$ as depicted below.  

![](images/68/68f70968b0dd256159dbfdcbfde4f2f63578237db1770e019c8fb19a5a638eaa.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \le r\le 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{4}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}{\int }_{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186157834 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-63ff2307-bdea-53b3-88e5-97b96d5ad36a" :answer/id #uuid "63ff2307-bdea-53b3-88e5-97b96d5ad36a"] "question-b842ef2a-5852-5df6-832b-3f42a5693c4d"] [17592186074970 :tutorial/content "A **unit rate** is a comparison of two quantities where one of the terms has a quantity of $1.$ This means the ratio, in fraction form, has a denominator of $1.$

For instance, suppose Michael earned $\[math] 200$ by selling $4$ identical tires.

The ratio of dollars to tires is ${\color{blue}200}:{\color{red}4}.$ Writing the ratio as a fraction, we have

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}200}}{{\color{red}4}} \, .
$$

The unit rate is how many dollars Michael got for $1$ tire.

We can make a denominator of $1$ by dividing the numerator and denominator by $4\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}200} \div 4}{{\color{red}4} \div 4} = \dfrac{{\color{blue}50}}{{\color{red}1}}
$$

This is the unit rate. In this case, we say that Michael got $\color{blue}50$ dollars *per* tire."] [17592186073975 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] [17592186161771 :question/problem "Which of the following matrices are symmetric?

["question-30380c91-5652-5051-8810-4fc9abb6a29f" :question/math-academy-id "q-96590"] ["question-30380c91-5652-5051-8810-4fc9abb6a29f" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

I. If $A$ is symmetric, then ${A}^{2}$ is always symmetric.

II. The sum of *any* two $n\times n$ matrices is always symmetric.

III. If $A$ is *any*  $n\times n$ matrix, then $A+{A}^{T}$ is always symmetric."] ["question-30380c91-5652-5051-8810-4fc9abb6a29f" :question/worked-solution "A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any symmetric matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(AA)^{T} & ={A}^{T}{A}^{T} \\  & =AA.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. As a counterexample, consider the matrices 

$\,$ $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].$ 

However, their sum is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+B & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any square matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+{A}^{T})^{T} & ={A}^{T}+({A}^{T})^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}+A \\  & =A+{A}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""] ["question-30380c91-5652-5051-8810-4fc9abb6a29f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] is **symmetric** if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A^T = A
$$

Equivalently, an $n\times n$ matrix is symmetric if $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all $1 \leq i,j\leq n.$

If $A$ is symmetric, this really means that it is symmetric across its main diagonal. 

For example, the matrix 

![](images/0f/0f62a89f8da1ab7bfb86d46fddb441e95e5e3a9554e5a88662691b4df40e19af.svg)

is symmetric since $A^T = A.$ 

On the other hand, the matrix

is not symmetric. Indeed, since $b_{12} \neq b_{21},$ we have $B^T \neq B.$"] [17592186163254 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $A$ is a symmetric matrix. Then, we have the following properties:

- $-A$ is symmetric

- $A^m$ is symmetric for any positive integer $m$

- $A^{-1}$ is symmetric for nonsingular $A$

If $A$ and $B$ are $n\times n$ symmetric matrices, we have the following properties:

- $A+B$ is symmetric

- The product $A\cdot B$ is *not* always symmetric. For example, if 
![](images/e4/e41d28b6c6562ada530024fe6ab29cc16447dce14b2f741b8b35758618c78103.svg)
then the product $A\cdot B$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A\cdot B & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

 
which is *not* symmetric.

Finally, the following two properties can be used to construct symmetric matrices:

- $A + A^T$ is symmetric for any *square* matrix $A$

By translating this into the language of vector spaces, we get the **rank-nullity theorem**. The rank-nullity theorem relates the rank of a matrix to the dimension of its null space:

*Let $A$ be a matrix (not necessarily square) with $n$ columns. Then,*

$$
\textrm{dim(Col}(A)) + \textrm{dim(Null}(A)) = \textrm{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n),
$$

*or, equivalently,*

$$
\textrm{rank}(A) + \textrm{nullity}(A) = n.
$$

For example, suppose that for some matrix $A,$ we have

![](images/30/30f6472f02a4ac47f285fff05e0cdbf56367acdd18231271dc3dccf0040901bd.svg)

We can use the rank-nullity theorem to calculate $\textrm{rank}(A).$

In this case, we must have $n=4,$ since this is the number of components in each of the vectors of the null space. 

Also, we must have $\textrm{nullity}(A)=2,$ since 
![](images/b5/b5f38590a71a2f8e1f29a5ba98920a10037737c1ebcbd3fd60f08a3e47555141.svg)

Therefore, using the rank-nullity theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A) & =n \\ \text{rank}(A)+2 & =4 \\ \text{rank}(A) & =4-2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186184421 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0]] "retractions" [[17592186180185 :question/answer-fields 17592186178654] [17592186180310 :question/problem "Given that $F(x, y) = ⟨x, x^{2}y⟩$ and $f(x, y) = xy$, calculate $∇ \cdot (fF)$."] [17592186179404 :answer-field/choices 17592186179408] [17592186179404 :answer-field/choices 17592186179409] [17592186179404 :answer-field/choices 17592186179405] [17592186179404 :answer-field/choices 17592186179406] [17592186179404 :answer-field/choices 17592186179407] [17592186180709 :tutorial/content "Recall that for functions $f(x)$ and $g(x),$ the product rule for differentiation is given by

$$

$$

There is an analogous rule for computing the divergence of the product of a vector field and a scalar field.

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field and $f$ is a scalar field. Then, we have the following identity:

$$
\nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf F) = f\, \nabla \cdot \mathbf {F}+  \mathbf F \cdot \nabla \! f
$$

 

where $\nabla f$ is the gradient of $f.$

Notice that the del operator $\nabla$ acts on the terms in the same way as the $\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}$ operator in the product rule for differentiation!

There are a few other tips that we can use to remember this rule:

$F(x, y) = x^{2}i - 2xyj$?"] [17592186177867 :answer-field/choices 17592186177868] [17592186177867 :answer-field/choices 17592186177869] [17592186177867 :answer-field/choices 17592186177870] [17592186177867 :answer-field/choices 17592186177871] [17592186180091 :question/answer-fields 17592186178215] [17592186180726 :tutorial/content "Let $\psi(x,y)$ be a two-variable function defined on a simply connected open set $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2.$ We know that for a point $(x_0,y_0)\in D,$ the vector

$$\left.\left(\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}\,\mathbf i -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}\,\mathbf j\right)\right|_{(x_0,y_0)}$$ is *tangential* to the level curve $\psi(x,y) = \psi(x_0,y_0).$

By computing this tangent vector at *every* point, we can generate a vector *field* tangential to the level curves of $\psi$ at every point.

With that in mind, let

$$\mathbf F(x,y)= P(x,y)\,\mathbf{i} + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf{j}$$

be a vector field defined on $D.$ A function $\psi(x,y)$ is said to be a **stream function** of $\mathbf F$ if it satisfies

$$P = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}, \qquad Q = -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}.$$

For example, let's consider the function

$$\psi(x,y) = x^2+y^2.$$

To construct a vector field with this stream function, we first compute the partial derivatives:

$$\begin{aligned}P & =\frac{∂ψ}{∂y} \\ & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) \\ & =2y, \\ Q & =-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x} \\ & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) \\ & =-2x.\end{aligned}$$

Thus, the vector field with the stream function $\psi$ is given by

$$\begin{aligned}F(x,y) & =P\,i+Q\,j=2y\,i-2x\,j.\end{aligned}$$

A diagram showing the surface $z = \psi(x,y),$ its level curves, and the vector field $\mathbf F$ are shown below.

![](images/69/696e6c623dbc3ecfae2643a7317d3d176294624289ecf6efb16debdc947d0394.png)

Note the following:

- The level curves of $\psi(x,y)$ are circles of the form $x^2+y^2=c$, and the vector field $\mathbf{F}$ in the $xy$-plane is tangential to these level curves.
- Suppose $\mathbf F$ represents the velocity of a fluid in the $xy$-plane. Then, the level curves of $\psi(x,y)$ represent the path of a massless particle in the $xy$-plane moving with the flow. For this reason, the level curves of $\psi$ are called **streamlines.**
- The stream function of a vector field is typically not unique since we can add any constant to $\psi$ to generate another valid stream function."] [17592186180763 :tutorial/content "Not all vector fields have an associated stream function! So, it's useful to have some way of determining whether a given vector field has a stream function or not. For this, we have the following theorem:

*Let $\mathbf F= P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ be a vector field defined in a simply connected open set $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2.$ The vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has a stream function $\psi(x,y)$ if and only if* $$\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.$$

In other words, the divergence of $\mathbf F$ must be zero everywhere for a stream function to exist.

We won't give a detailed proof of this result here, but it's quite easy to see why it may be true.

Recall that if $\psi(x,y)$ is a stream function of $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ if it satisfies

$$P = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}, \qquad Q = -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}.$$

Calculating the divergence of this vector field, we get

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{∂ψ}{∂y})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}) \\ & =\frac{{∂}^{2}ψ}{∂x∂y}-\frac{{∂}^{2}ψ}{∂y∂x} \\ & =\frac{{∂}^{2}ψ}{∂x∂y}-\frac{{∂}^{2}ψ}{∂x∂y} \\ & =0\end{aligned}$$"] [17592186180759 :tutorial/content "Let's find a stream function for the following vector field:

$$\mathbf{F}(x,y) = e^x \sin y\,\mathbf{i} + e^x \cos y\,\mathbf{j}$$

Note that our vector field $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ has the simply connected domain $D=\mathbb{R}^2,$ where

$$P(x,y) = e^x\sin y, \qquad Q(x,y) = e^x\cos y.$$

Let's start by checking that a stream function exists. Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}y.\end{aligned}$$

Hence, $\mathbf F$ has a stream function since $\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $\psi(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $\mathbf F= P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ if

$$P = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}, \qquad Q = -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}.$$

In our case, we have

$$\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y} = e^x\sin y, \qquad \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} = -e^x\cos y.$$

To find a stream function, we **partially integrate** these two equations and compare the results:

- For the first equation, we have $$\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y} = e^x\sin y$$ Partially integrating this equation with respect to $y$ (that is, treating $x$ as though it were a constant), we get $$\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}y\,\text{d}y+f(x) \\ & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}y+f(x),\end{aligned}$$ where $f$ is an arbitrary function.
- For the second equation, we have $$\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} = -e^x\cos y.$$ Partially integrating this equation with respect to $x$ (that is, treating $y$ as though it were a constant), we get $$\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =\int -{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}y\,\text{d}x+g(y) \\ & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}y+g(y)\end{aligned}$$ where $g$ is an arbitrary function.

Comparing our two expressions for $\psi,$ we get equality by setting $f=g=0.$ Therefore, we have

$$\psi(x,y) = -e^x \cos y.$$

Finally, remember that the streamlines of $\mathbf F$ are given by the level curves of $\psi.$ So, to find the streamlines of $\mathbf F,$ we plot the curves $\psi = k$ for different values of $k.$ The level curves of $\psi$ are always tangential to $\mathbf F.$"] [17592186054601 :question/problem "Which of the given points is a solution to $y=-2x+1$?

$$

$$

the partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u+v} & \\,\\frac{∂x}{∂v} & ={e}^{u+v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & ={e}^{u-v} & \\,\\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-{e}^{u-v}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} & {e}^{u+v} \\\\ {e}^{u-v} & -{e}^{u-v}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & ={e}^{u+v}\\cdot (-{e}^{u-v})-{e}^{u+v}\\cdot {e}^{u-v} \\\\  & =-{e}^{2u}-{e}^{2u} \\\\  & =-2{e}^{2u}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, when $[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}0 \\\\ -5\\end{aligned}],$ the value of our But for now, it is sufficient to know that \n\n- $\\mathbf T$ takes points (or vectors) from the $uv$-plane as input and maps them to points (vectors) in the $xy$-plane, and\n\n- rectangular regions {:db/id 17592186130225 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130460 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\\mathbf{T}: U \\to \\mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation given by\n\n![](images/f9/f9a1c3375eed570284c4e001f119f21901f4493a0b851919b92b678a74187444.svg) \n\nWe'll assume that $\\mathbf T$ is a $\\boldsymbol{C}^1$ **transformation**, which means that  $x$ and $y$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on an open set $U$ contained in $\\Bbb R^2.$ \n\nThe **Jacobian determinant** of $\\mathbf T,$ denoted $\\dfrac{\\partial (x, y)}{\\partial (u, v)} ,$ is defined as\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}|=\\frac{∂x}{∂u}\\cdot In such cases, a rectangle in the $uv$-plane collapses to either a line segment or point in the $xy$-plane.\n\n![](images/9a/9a038c5de0e9f3205194fd7941a4b371c695c51c294f2ad5ac0b8fc1015811d1.png)\n\n![](images/98/9813ba294a0242abbfb885ebd3e82505d05a2f8a1cfa3975c7859f9530cac8b1.png)\n\nAffine transformations are special because these properties are *global*. In other words, they apply *everywhere* in the plane. So, for example, if $\\textrm{det}(T) = 2$, then the image of *every* rectangle in the $uv$-plane is a parallelogram with double the area of its preimage." :tutorial/id #uuid "4dcb1ce1-bfad-524c-a89a-a589532a1067" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7672 :tutorial/title "A Review of Affine Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "c956f456-bd29-5cf7-83bd-de9b757b718f" :step/math-academy-id 44557 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130227}} {:db/id 17592186130227 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130462 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.\n\nThe critical difference is that, in general, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. \n\nTo understand what this means, suppose that $\\mathbf{T}: U \\to \\mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation, where\n![](images/d0/d0149013f12e5cdad31611d4c64489c0aaf6049707e9eed22202ae70d2d8a38a.svg) \n\nand we assume that $x(u,v)$ and $y(u,v)$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on $U.$\n\nFor ease of notation, let's introduce $J(u_0,v_0)$ to denote the Jacobian determinant of $\\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0){:}$\n\n$$\nJ(u_0,v_0) = \\left.\\dfrac{\\partial(x,y)}{\\partial(u,v)}\\right|_{(u_0,v_0)}\n$$\n\nLet's describe $\\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangle in the $uv$-plane whose bottom-left corner is the point $(u_0,v_0).$\n\n![](images/dc/dc084ec02cd0c4fac71379590e8dc4973354cacc898e267a0eb15a6e8500f31f.png)\n\nIt's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the $xy$-plane is typically *not* a parallelogram! However, provided that our rectangle is very small, its image can be *approximated* by a parallelogram (we'll justify this in a future lesson). \n\nThe Jacobian determinant of $\\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangle and its (approximate) image:\n\n- The *local* area scale factor of $\\mathbf T$. \n\nSuppose the length and width of our rectangle are $\\delta u$ and $\\delta v,$ so its area is $\\delta A = \\delta u\\delta v.$ Then, it can be shown that the parallelogram in the $xy$-plane has an area equal to $\\left|J(u_0,v_0)\\right| \\cdot \\delta A.$\n\n![](images/be/be1771ebb041c418c58d7d5615510e2fcacfeaf3677fbace739498ef1998ef11.png)\n\nNote the similarity of this formula with that of affine transformations described earlier (we've simply replaced $\\det(T)$ with the Jacobian).\n\n- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)> 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving.\n\n![](images/8c/8c649fdd526a831fb990393b292fb4582dad14c2391d129e9ed59792ebb8ac31.png)\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)<  0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.\n\n![](images/ae/ae5a3d0a42e1c4b9f692994b89815382a30cdf3e676bbd9844258ad2a6961608.png)\n\n- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)\\neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.\n\n![](images/33/33ca98206a347e13aa8ec179a52dd755008d9a7d74882391e0c3f2344f6f6641.png)\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.\n\n![](images/3d/3d4534c263a9a5bb26ba35ce8f879cf01db741441d948c023acaa9407d58e6e0.png)\n\n![](images/65/659f26ac6aba808d66a760d5683f265fd7c54431d894b2eabdc255b46368fc24.png)\n\nPoints $(u_0,v_0)$ such that $J(u_0,v_0)=0$ are called **critical points.** Critical points are very important. We'll discuss these in more detail in future lessons.\n\nWe again stress that the Jacobian describes *local* properties, that is, local to the point $(u_0,v_0).$ The effect of a nonlinear transformation on an object varies as we move around the $uv$-plane, so its local properties also vary. So, for example, if a transformation is orientation-preserving at one point, it does *not* mean it's orientation-preserving everywhere!" :tutorial/id #uuid "3f6a2c63-d9fc-533c-8c4b-fd822216f0f1" =|\\begin{aligned}\\operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\\\ \\operatorname{sin}⁡v & u\\operatorname{cos}⁡v\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =\\operatorname{cos}⁡v\\cdot (u\\operatorname{cos}⁡v)-(-u\\operatorname{sin}⁡v)\\cdot \\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\\\  & =u{cos}^{2}⁡v+u{sin}^{2}⁡v \\\\  & =u({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\\\  & =u.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nWe'll spend some time discussing the meaning behind the Jacobian shortly. But for now, let's get some practice at computing it." :tutorial/id #uuid "f0ea7366-d3d6-5645-99d8-72f7febb8d19" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7668 :tutorial/title "The Jacobian Determinant"} {:db/id 17592186130461 :tutorial/content "To understand what the Jacobian describes, we recall our knowledge of affine transformations.\n\nConsider the affine transformation $\\mathbf T:\\Bbb R^2 \\to \\Bbb R^2,$ defined by the matrix equation \n\n$$\n\\mathbf x = T\\mathbf u + \\mathbf b,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\mathbf u, \\mathbf b,$ and $\\mathbf x$ are vectors from $\\mathbb R^2,$ and $T$ is a $2\\times 2$ matrix. \n\nFor an affine transformation, the determinant of $T$ gives us the following information:\n\n- The *area scale factor* of the transformation:\n\nIf a rectangle in the $uv$-plane has area $A,$ its image in the $xy$-plane is a parallelogram of area $|\\det(T)|\\cdot A.$\n\n![](images/04/04f36d98bf7589d1faadeffee0812590337fd36d8bb44f5abe1920948dee5bb0.png)\n\n- Whether the transformation is *orientation-preserving* or *orientation-reversing:*\n\nIf $\\textrm{det}(T) > 0,$ the transformation is orientation-preserving.\n\n![](images/49/496a49ee541eab31f69f9c571e450547b0c6942b100bc8e24fbd927dd43e4d33.png)\n\nIf $\\textrm{det}(T) < 0,$ the transformation is orientation-reversing.\n\n![](images/21/211369d6f3fc70bcf7cf40f3270c24c245d306247efc429cb85589e42c19ee07.png)\n\n- Whether the transformation is *invertible* or *non-invertible:*\n\nIf $\\textrm{det}(T) \\neq 0,$ the transformation is invertible.\n\n![](images/e4/e4b840ad5a3efa082ac4056d1d9b7c03d2e3e11e016e053df055dbb2b39f0d1f.png)\n\nIf $\\textrm{det}(T) = 0,$ the transformation is non-invertible. In such cases, a rectangle in the $uv$-plane collapses to either a line segment or point in the $xy$-plane.\n\n![](images/9a/9a038c5de0e9f3205194fd7941a4b371c695c51c294f2ad5ac0b8fc1015811d1.png)\n\n![](images/98/9813ba294a0242abbfb885ebd3e82505d05a2f8a1cfa3975c7859f9530cac8b1.png)\n\nAffine transformations are special because these properties are *global*. In other words, they apply *everywhere* in the plane. So, for example, if $\\textrm{det}(T) = 2$, then the image of *every* rectangle in the $uv$-plane is a parallelogram with double the area of its preimage." :tutorial/id #uuid "4dcb1ce1-bfad-524c-a89a-a589532a1067" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7672 :tutorial/title "A Review of Affine Transformations"} {:db/id 17592186130227 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130462 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.\n\nThe critical difference is that, in general, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. \n\nTo understand what this means, suppose that $\\mathbf{T}: U \\to \\mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation, where\n![](images/d0/d0149013f12e5cdad31611d4c64489c0aaf6049707e9eed22202ae70d2d8a38a.svg) \n\nand we assume that $x(u,v)$ and $y(u,v)$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on $U.$\n\nFor ease of notation, let's introduce $J(u_0,v_0)$ to denote the Jacobian determinant of $\\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0){:}$\n\n$$\nJ(u_0,v_0) = \\left.\\dfrac{\\partial(x,y)}{\\partial(u,v)}\\right|_{(u_0,v_0)}\n$$\n\nLet's describe $\\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangle in the $uv$-plane whose bottom-left corner is the point $(u_0,v_0).$\n\n![](images/dc/dc084ec02cd0c4fac71379590e8dc4973354cacc898e267a0eb15a6e8500f31f.png)\n\nIt's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the $xy$-plane is typically *not* a parallelogram! However, provided that our rectangle is very small, its image can be *approximated* by a parallelogram (we'll justify this in a future lesson). \n\nThe Jacobian determinant of $\\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangle and its (approximate) image:\n\n- The *local* area scale factor of $\\mathbf T$. \n\nSuppose the length and width of our rectangle are $\\delta u$ and $\\delta v,$ so its area is $\\delta A = \\delta u\\delta v.$ Then, it can be shown that the parallelogram in the $xy$-plane has an area equal to $\\left|J(u_0,v_0)\\right| \\cdot \\delta A.$\n\n![](images/be/be1771ebb041c418c58d7d5615510e2fcacfeaf3677fbace739498ef1998ef11.png)\n\nNote the similarity of this formula with that of affine transformations described earlier (we've simply replaced $\\det(T)$ with the Jacobian).\n\n- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)> 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving.\n\n![](images/8c/8c649fdd526a831fb990393b292fb4582dad14c2391d129e9ed59792ebb8ac31.png)\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)<  0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.\n\n![](images/ae/ae5a3d0a42e1c4b9f692994b89815382a30cdf3e676bbd9844258ad2a6961608.png)\n\n- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)\\neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.\n\n![](images/33/33ca98206a347e13aa8ec179a52dd755008d9a7d74882391e0c3f2344f6f6641.png)\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.\n\n![](images/3d/3d4534c263a9a5bb26ba35ce8f879cf01db741441d948c023acaa9407d58e6e0.png)\n\n![](images/65/659f26ac6aba808d66a760d5683f265fd7c54431d894b2eabdc255b46368fc24.png)\n\nPoints $(u_0,v_0)$ such that $J(u_0,v_0)=0$ are called **critical points.** Critical points are very important. We'll discuss these in more detail in future lessons.\n\nWe again stress that the Jacobian describes *local* properties, that is, local to the point $(u_0,v_0).$ The effect of a nonlinear transformation on an object varies as we move around the $uv$-plane, so its local properties also vary. So, for example, if a transformation is orientation-preserving at one point, it does *not* mean it's orientation-preserving everywhere!" :tutorial/id #uuid "3f6a2c63-d9fc-533c-8c4b-fd822216f0f1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7673 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind the Jacobian"} :step/id #uuid "0e6a94d3-c32f-5582-98ea-69a8605ef653" :step/math-academy-id 44558 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130230}} {:db/id 17592186130462 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.\n\nThe critical difference is that, in general, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. \n\nTo understand what this means, suppose that $\\mathbf{T}: U \\to \\mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation, where\n![](images/d0/d0149013f12e5cdad31611d4c64489c0aaf6049707e9eed22202ae70d2d8a38a.svg) \n\nand we assume that $x(u,v)$ and $y(u,v)$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on $U.$\n\nFor ease of notation, let's introduce $J(u_0,v_0)$ to denote the Jacobian determinant of $\\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0){:}$\n\n$$\nJ(u_0,v_0) = \\left.\\dfrac{\\partial(x,y)}{\\partial(u,v)}\\right|_{(u_0,v_0)}\n$$\n\nLet's describe $\\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangle in the $uv$-plane whose bottom-left corner is the point $(u_0,v_0).$\n\n![](images/dc/dc084ec02cd0c4fac71379590e8dc4973354cacc898e267a0eb15a6e8500f31f.png)\n\nIt's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the $xy$-plane is typically *not* a parallelogram! \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}-\\operatorname{sin}⁡u & -2v \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =(-\\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\\cdot 1-1\\cdot (-2v) \\\\  & =-\\operatorname{sin}⁡u+2v \\\\ {\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(0,3)} & =(-\\operatorname{sin}⁡u+2v)\\,{|}_{u=0\\,v=3} \\\\  & =-\\operatorname{sin}⁡0+2(3) \\\\  & =6\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:\n\n$$\n\\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\\cdot {{\\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\\delta A}\n$$\n\n \n\nComputing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}1 & 2v \\\\ \\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) & \\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =1\\cdot \\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)-\\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\\cdot 2v \\\\  & =(1-2v)\\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\\\ {\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-3,3)} & =(1-2v)\\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\\,{|}_{u=-3\\,v=3} \\\\  & =(1-2(3))\\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3+3) \\\\  & =-5\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-5|\\cdot \\delta A \\\\  & =5\\,\\delta A.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/math-academy-id 33326} {:db/id 17592186180420 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180689 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $\\mathbf F = P\\,\\mathbf i + Q\\,\\mathbf j + R\\,\\mathbf k$ is a vector field on $\\mathbb R^3,$ then the divergence of $\\mathbf F$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\textrm{div}\\,\\mathbf F = \\nabla\\cdot \\mathbf F = \\dfrac{\\partial P}{\\partial x} + \\dfrac{\\partial Q}{\\partial y} + \\dfrac{\\partial R}{\\partial z}.\n$$\n\nSince divergence is computed using derivatives, it's unsurprising that it shares similar properties with derivatives.\n\nFor example, if $\\mathbf F$ and $\\mathbf H$ are vector fields and $k$ is a scalar constant, then we have the following linearity properties:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & ∇\\cdot (k\\,F)=k\\,(∇\\cdot F) \\\\  & ∇\\cdot (F+H)=∇\\cdot F+∇\\cdot H\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nApplying these rules can often help us to save time when computing divergence. Let's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "f5f31027-65f9-53ab-bd9a-c3454d049b07" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5529 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6062f3c7-6f7f-55fd-81a5-fe282d53dde8" :step/math-academy-id 34372 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180411}} {:db/id 17592186180471 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180709 :tutorial/content "Recall that for functions $f(x)$ and $g(x),$ the product rule for differentiation is given by\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\textrm d }{\\textrm d x}(f\\cdot g) = f\\dfrac{\\textrm d }{\\textrm d x}(g) +  g\\dfrac{\\textrm d }{\\textrm d x}(f).\n$$\n\nThere is an analogous rule for computing the divergence of the product of a vector field and a scalar field.\n\nSuppose that $\\mathbf F$ is a vector field and $f$ is a scalar field. Then, we have the following identity:\n\n$$\n\\nabla \\cdot (f\\,\\mathbf F) = f\\, \\nabla \\cdot \\mathbf {F}+  \\mathbf F \\cdot \\nabla \\! f\n$$\n\n \n\nwhere $\\nabla f$ is the gradient of $f.$\n\nNotice that the del operator $\\nabla$ acts on the terms in the same way as the $\\dfrac{\\textrm d}{\\textrm d x}$ operator in the product rule for differentiation!\n\nThere are a few other tips that we can use to remember this rule:\n\n- The term $\\nabla \\cdot (f\\,\\mathbf F)$ on the left-hand side must be a scalar field because it's a divergence. So, the two terms on the right-hand side must be scalar fields, too.\n\n- The term $f\\, \\nabla \\cdot \\mathbf {F}$ on the right-hand side is a scalar field because both $f$ and $\\nabla \\cdot \\mathbf F$ are scalar fields, and the product of two scalar fields is a scalar field. Note that this \"product\" is just regular multiplication.\n\n- The term $\\mathbf F \\cdot \\nabla \\! f$ on the right-hand side is a scalar field because both $\\mathbf F$ and $\\nabla f$ are *vector* fields, and the *dot product* of two vector fields is a scalar field." :tutorial/id #uuid "c0316ea0-9d48-5155-82e8-948d53b0f677" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5795 :tutorial/title "The Product Rule for Divergence"} :step/id #uuid "6797ef0f-9f84-5dda-8b36-6c76a5fe635c" :step/math-academy-id 35539 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180414}}] :activity/title "Properties of the Divergence Operator" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179855} {:db/id 17592186180420 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180689 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $\\mathbf F = P\\,\\mathbf i + Q\\,\\mathbf j + R\\,\\mathbf k$ is a vector field on $\\mathbb R^3,$ then the divergence of $\\mathbf F$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\textrm{div}\\,\\mathbf F = \\nabla\\cdot \\mathbf F = \\dfrac{\\partial P}{\\partial x} + \\dfrac{\\partial Q}{\\partial y} + \\dfrac{\\partial R}{\\partial z}.\n$$\n\nSince divergence is computed using derivatives, it's unsurprising that it shares similar properties with derivatives.\n\nFor example, if $\\mathbf F$ and $\\mathbf H$ are vector fields and $k$ is a scalar constant, then we have the following linearity properties:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & ∇\\cdot (k\\,F)=k\\,(∇\\cdot F) \\\\  & ∇\\cdot (F+H)=∇\\cdot F+∇\\cdot H\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nApplying these rules can often help us to save time when computing divergence. Let's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "f5f31027-65f9-53ab-bd9a-c3454d049b07" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5529 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186180709 :tutorial/content "Recall that for functions $f(x)$ and $g(x),$ the product rule for differentiation is given by\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\textrm d }{\\textrm d x}(f\\cdot g) = f\\dfrac{\\textrm d }{\\textrm d x}(g) +  g\\dfrac{\\textrm d }{\\textrm d x}(f).\n$$\n\nThere is an analogous rule for computing the divergence of the product of a vector field and a scalar field.\n\nSuppose that $\\mathbf F$ is a vector field and $f$ is a scalar field. Then, we have the following identity:\n\n$$\n\\nabla \\cdot (f\\,\\mathbf F) = f\\, \\nabla \\cdot \\mathbf {F}+  \\mathbf F \\cdot \\nabla \\! f\n$$\n\n \n\nwhere $\\nabla f$ is the gradient of $f.$\n\nNotice that the del operator $\\nabla$ acts on the terms in the same way as the $\\dfrac{\\textrm d}{\\textrm d x}$ operator in the product rule for differentiation!\n\nThere are a few other tips that we can use to remember this rule:\n\n- The term $\\nabla \\cdot (f\\,\\mathbf F)$ on the left-hand side must be a scalar field because it's a divergence. So, the two terms on the right-hand side must be scalar fields, too.\n\n- The term $f\\, \\nabla \\cdot \\mathbf {F}$ on the right-hand side is a scalar field because both $f$ and $\\nabla \\cdot \\mathbf F$ are scalar fields, and the product of two scalar fields is a scalar field. Note that this \"product\" is just regular multiplication.\n\n- The term $\\mathbf F \\cdot \\nabla \\! f$ on the right-hand side is a scalar field because both $\\mathbf F$ and $\\nabla f$ are *vector* fields, and the *dot product* of two vector fields is a scalar field." :tutorial/id #uuid "c0316ea0-9d48-5155-82e8-948d53b0f677" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5795 :tutorial/title "The Product :step/content {:db/id 17592186065441 :tutorial/content "When we want to calculate the **square of a binomial**, like\n\n$$\n(a+b)^2,\n$$\n\nthere's a formula that we can use instead of working out the product $(a+b)(a+b)$ manually. The formula is\n\n$$\n(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2.\n$$\n\nIt might be helpful to remember this as *\"the square of the first term, plus the square of the second term, plus twice the product.\"*\n\nSuppose we need to calculate the square $(x+3)^2.$ In this case, we have $a= x$ and $b=3.$ We substitute into the formula and simplify:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2} & = \\\\ (x)^{2}+2(x)(3)+(3)^{2} & = \\\\ {x}^{2}+6x+9 & \\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe can check that the formula gives the correct result by working out the multiplication manually:\n\n$$\n\\eqalign{\n\t\t(x + 3)^2 &= \\[3pt]\n\t\t(x + 3)(x + 3) &= \\[3pt]\n\t\tx(x + 3) + 3(x + 3) &= \\[3pt]\n\t\tx^2 + 3x + 3x + 9 &= \\[3pt]\n\t\tx^2 + 6x + 9 &\\, {\\color{green}{\\checkmark}}\n\t}\n$$\n\nSo we get the same result! But by using the formula, we save a lot of time and effort." :tutorial/id #uuid "0266d886-b5db-53fe-bc51-f6486beb6eef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8878 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "ee3a0134-3957-5b1c-b05a-a30af1c8709d" :step/math-academy-id 170779 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065098}} {:db/id 17592186065098 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064232 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063991 :question/id #uuid "70f19ea4-d0b8-537a-8ae4-06a236cf37cf" :question/math-academy-id "e-14318"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "288c08af-0583-5588-b767-4254544cf70c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050818}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064590} {:db/id 17592186064678} {:db/id 17592186064749} {:db/id 17592186482538} {:db/id 17592186482578}] :knowledge-point/title "Squaring Linear Binomials"} :step/id #uuid "39924b31-d2c9-5359-be1b-3c04f7ad4699" :step/math-academy-id 170780 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065099}} {:db/id 17592186065099 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064233 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063992 :question/id #uuid "c1a6df9e-b1e8-51c8-b5df-4cc624e14193" :question/math-academy-id "e-14319"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "63291c46-6a0f-5e7c-ab0a-acba80fe58f3" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064592} {:db/id 17592186064593} {:db/id 17592186064729} {:db/id 17592186482519} {:db/id 17592186482545} {:db/id 17592186482593} {:db/id 17592186482604}] :knowledge-point/title "Squaring Nonlinear Binomials"} :step/id #uuid "9b092f72-50ae-5b82-96c3-f01cc623e041" :step/math-academy-id 170784 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065100}} {:db/id 17592186065100 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065442 :tutorial/content "So far, we've been using the formula for the square of a binomial involving addition:\n\n$$\n(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2\n$$\n\nThere is also a similar formula that we can use to compute the square of a binomial involving subtraction. The formula is\n\n$$\n(a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2.\n$$\n\nFor example, to compute the square $(x-3)^2,$ we can substitute $a=x$ and $b=3$ into the formula and simplify:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}(x-3)^{2} & = \\\\ (x)^{2}-2(x)(3)+(3)^{2} & = \\\\ {x}^{2}-6x+9 & \\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe can check that the formula gives the correct result by working out the multiplication manually:\n\n$$\n\\eqalign{\n\t\t(x - 3)^2 &= \\\n\t\t(x - 3)(x - 3) &= \\\n\t\tx(x - 3) - 3(x - 3) &= \\\n\t\tx^2 - 3x - 3x + 9 &= \\\n\t\tx^2 - 6x + 9 &\\, {\\color{green}{\\checkmark}}\n\t}\n$$\n\nAgain, we get the same result." :tutorial/id #uuid "e42b96f5-ca3b-588b-8931-106b975bd0ac" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8879 :tutorial/title "Binomials With Subtraction"} :step/id #uuid "13d60779-951a-5265-8019-e1ca3444406c" :step/math-academy-id 170788 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065101}} {:db/id 17592186065101 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064234 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063993 :question/id #uuid "487f1c4c-63c9-51cf-9a0e-7d9bc0a4c7c7" :question/math-academy-id "e-14320"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "afd30bc7-dce9-5e03-a213-2b9695e39091" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064591} {:db/id 17592186064594} {:db/id 17592186064679} {:db/id 17592186482554} {:db/id 17592186482594}] :knowledge-point/title "Squaring Binomials With Subtraction"} :step/id #uuid "2fb2e377-ee0a-5a7e-a9fc-c5e5d9b5786a" :step/math-academy-id 170789}] :activity/title "Squaring Binomials" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186064447} {:db/id 17592186065097 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065441 :tutorial/content "When we want to calculate the **square of a binomial**, like\n\n$$\n(a+b)^2,\n$$\n\nthere's a formula that we can use instead of working out the product $(a+b)(a+b)$ manually. [\\begin{aligned}k-10 \\\\ -6+5k\\end{aligned}] & =[\\begin{aligned}-4k \\\\ 2k\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis gives us the following system of linear equations:\n\n$$\n{\\begin{aligned}k-10=-4k, \\\\ -6+5k=2k\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSolving for $k$ in the first equation, we get\n\n$$\nk-10=-4k\\,⟹\\,k=2.\n$$\n\nNow, substituting $k=2$ into the second equation, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}-6+5k & =2k \\\\ -6+5(2) & =2(2) \\\\ 4 & =4,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhich is a true statement.\n\nTherefore, the solution of the system is $k=2.$"} {:db/id Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of correct answers that the student gets.\n\nHere, we have the following information:\n\n- there are $n=12$ questions\n\n- the probability of hitting each question is $p=50%=0.5$\n\nSo, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(12,0.5).$ We want to find the probability of getting $x=10$ correct answers.\n\nThe number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function\n\n$$\nP(X=x)=(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},\n$$\n\nwhere $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.\n\nSubstituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X=10) & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{10})(0.5)^{10}(1-0.5)^{12-10} \\\\  & =\\frac{12!}{10!(12-10)!}(0.5)^{10}(0.5)^{2} \\\\  & =66(0.5)^{10}(0.5)^{2} \\\\  & =0.016\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nrounded to $3$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186420373 :question/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "A box of chocolates contains cherry creams and almond little cakes in the ratio of $2:1.$ Four chocolates are selected at random, with replacement. What is the probability of getting at most $2$ cherry creams? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be the number of selected cherry creams.\n\nHere, we have the following information:\n\n- there are $n=4$ selected chocolates\n\n- since cherry creams and almond little cakes are in the ratio of $2:1,$ the probability of selecting a cherry cream from the box is $p=\\frac{2}{3}$\n\nSo, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(4,\\frac{2}{3}).$ \n\nThe number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function\n\n$$\nP(X=x)=(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},\n$$\n\nwhere $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.\n\nSubstituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{x}){(\\frac{2}{3})}^{x}{(1-\\frac{2}{3})}^{4-x} \\\\  & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{x}){(\\frac{2}{3})}^{x}{(\\frac{1}{3})}^{4-x}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe want to find the probability of getting at most $2$ cherry creams. So, we compute\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X\\le 2) & =P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2) \\\\  & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{0}){(\\frac{2}{3})}^{0}{(\\frac{1}{3})}^{4-0}+(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{1}){(\\frac{2}{3})}^{1}{(\\frac{1}{3})}^{4-1}+(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{2}){(\\frac{2}{3})}^{2}{(\\frac{1}{3})}^{4-2} \\\\  & =1{(\\frac{2}{3})}^{0}{(\\frac{1}{3})}^{4}+4{(\\frac{2}{3})}^{1}{(\\frac{1}{3})}^{3}+6{(\\frac{2}{3})}^{2}{(\\frac{1}{3})}^{2} \\\\  & ≈0.407\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nrounded to $3$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186304923 :question/id #uuid "64469c0a-c9a4-5634-8d45-1147a1381d27" :question/math-academy-id "q-331526"} {:db/id 17592186354340 :question/id #uuid "fac74754-68c7-525c-973a-4d985a07fcb5" :question/math-academy-id "q-84787"} {:db/id 17592186411560 :question/id #uuid "265e293f-7554-5958-abfd-df783c671c82" :question/math-academy-id "q-89399"} {:db/id 17592186411564 :question/id #uuid "69ccd3d4-6bc6-5b97-931d-42636fcb0b40" :question/math-academy-id "q-130748"} {:db/id 17592186411569 :question/id #uuid "90500394-6fc0-5ba4-a5dc-ea52dd5425de" :question/math-academy-id "q-89398"} {:db/id 17592186411575 :question/id #uuid "ec42c1b6-69ea-5d9d-b8b5-5ad8c82e5789" :question/math-academy-id "q-331525"} {:db/id 17592186411576 :question/id #uuid "f0df1382-8e7a-5174-b609-3e041c2744d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-84797"} {:db/id 17592186420372 :question/id #uuid "2532926b-6b81-5b1e-a7b4-0b4cbbf77029" :question/math-academy-id "q-276040" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c7a3a7fc-b93c-517e-bc20-23ebc61bbf16" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.737" :db/id 17592186420363}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186420363} :answer-field/id #uuid "d29ba2bc-6b0d-55f1-9a0b-b4874a45e108" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186420370}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "An unfair coin has an $80%$ chance of landing on heads. The coin is tossed $5$ times. Rounded to $3$ decimal places, what is the probability that the coin landed on heads at least four times?\n\nRounded to $3$ decimal places, the probability is\n{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times the coin landed on heads.\n\nHere, we have the following information:\n\n- There are $n=5$ tosses.\n\n- The probability of landing on heads is $p=80%=0.8.$\n\nSo, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(5,0.8).$ \n\nThe number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function\n\n$$\nP(X=x)=(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},\n$$\n\nwhere $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.\n\nSubstituting the above information into the formula for the probability mass function, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x})(0.8)^{x}(1-0.8)^{5-x} \\\\  & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x})(0.8)^{x}(0.2)^{5-x}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe want to find the probability that the coin landed on heads at least $4$ of the $5$ games. So, we compute\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X\\ge 4) & =P(X=4)+P(X=5) \\\\  & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{4})(0.8)^{4}(1-0.8)^{5-4}+(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{5})(0.8)^{5}(1-0.8)^{5-5} \\\\  & =5(0.8)^{4}(0.2)+1(0.8)^{5} \\\\  & ≈0.737,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nrounded to $3$ decimal places"} {:db/id 17592186435653 :question/id #uuid "02d7c8e8-c1c1-5349-b786-2cc03d634147" :question/math-academy-id "q-331528" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fca83564-ebe2-59c0-a75f-f0b7a4ff3ff4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.683" :db/id 17592186435647}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435647} :answer-field/id #uuid "d40b2fb2-406e-5639-97e3-0ab4b3c53608" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186435651}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "A quality‑check sensor detects a flaw with probability $40%.$ If $5$ items are inspected, rounded to $3$ decimal places, what is the probability that at most $2$ of them contain a flaw?\n\nRounded to $3$ decimal places, the probability is\n{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of flawed items detected.\n\nHere, we have the following information:\n\n- There are $n=5$ items.\n\n- The probability of a flaw is $p=40%=0.4.$\n\nSo, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(5,0.4).$\n\nThe number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function\n\n$$\nP(X=x)=(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},\n$$\n\nwhere $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.\n\nSubstituting the above information into the formula for the probability mass function, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x})(0.4)^{x}(1-0.4)^{5-x} \\\\  & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x})(0.4)^{x}(0.6)^{5-x}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe want to find the probability that at most $2$ of the $5$ items contain flaws. So, we compute\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X\\le 2) & =P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2) \\\\  & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{0})(0.4)^{0}(0.6)^{5}+(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{1})(0.4)^{1}(0.6)^{4}+(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{2})(0.4)^{2}(0.6)^{3} \\\\  & =1(0.6)^{5}+5(0.4)(0.6)^{4}+10(0.4)^{2}(0.6)^{3} \\\\  & ≈0.683,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nrounded to $3$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186435656 :question/id #uuid "c1276b85-cb47-56f4-9380-ccdb52fdaba5" :question/math-academy-id "q-89400" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2ebbeff3-c5ba-5410-a408-4b1fcdd81dd9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.452" :db/id 17592186435636} {:answer/id #uuid "318f6f4d-16fa-51e6-b179-78e91115f020" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.254" :db/id 17592186435637} {:answer/id #uuid "87d0f7be-dc1b-5137-82d6-ad06ca042afd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.524" :db/id 17592186435640} {:answer/id #uuid "90044cbf-45a0-57af-832e-49250df1a7d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.555" :db/id 17592186435642} {:answer/id #uuid "f5b00b74-2769-5031-9b6b-ad1e823bdbaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.444" :db/id 17592186435645}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435642} :answer-field/id #uuid "27c18810-179b-53f0-a245-19fdca7de9b4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435648}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "In a coffee shop, $28%$ of the customers order their coffee to go. Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of customers that order their coffee to go.\n\nHere, we have the following information:\n\n- there are $n=12$ customers\n\n- the probability that each customer orders the coffee to go is $p=28%=0.28$\n\nSo, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(12,0.28).$\n\nThe number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function\n\n$$\nP(X=x)=(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},\n$$\n\nwhere $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.\n\nSubstituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{x}){(0.28)}^{x}{(1-0.28)}^{12-x} \\\\  & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{x}){(0.28)}^{x}{(0.72)}^{12-x}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe want to find the probability of getting a \"success\" (i.e., the customer orders the coffee to go) on at most $3$ trials. So, we compute\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X\\le 3) & =P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2)+P(X=3) \\\\  & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{0}){(0.28)}^{0}{(0.72)}^{12}+(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{1}){(0.28)}^{1}{(0.72)}^{11}+(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{2}){(0.28)}^{2}{(0.72)}^{10}+(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{3}){(0.28)}^{3}{(0.72)}^{9} \\\\  & ={(0.28)}^{0}{(0.72)}^{12}+12{(0.28)}^{1}{(0.72)}^{11}+66{(0.28)}^{2}{(0.72)}^{10}+220{(0.28)}^{3}{(0.72)}^{9} \\\\  & =0.555\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nrounded to $3$ decimal places."} {:db/id The camera is triggered $7$ times during the night. Rounded to $3$ decimal places, what is the probability that it detects an animal at least $3$ times?\n\nRounded to $3$ decimal places, the probability is\n{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times the camera successfully detected an animal.\n\nHere, we have the following information:\n\n- There are $n=7$ triggers.\n\n- The probability of detection is $p=40%=0.4.$\n\nSo, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(7,0.4).$\n\nThe number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function\n\n$$\nP(X=x)=(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},\n$$\n\nwhere $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.\n\nSubstituting the above information into the formula for the probability mass function, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{x})(0.4)^{x}(1-0.4)^{7-x} \\\\  & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{x})(0.4)^{x}(0.6)^{7-x}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe want to find the probability of detecting an animal at least $3$ times. This corresponds to $P(X\\ge 3).$\n\nHowever, computing\n\n$$\nP(X\\ge 3)=P(X=3)+P(X=4)+…+P(X=7)\n$$\n\nwill involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X\\ge 3) & =1-P(X<3) \\\\  & =1-[P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2)] \\\\  & =1-[(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{0})(0.4)^{0}(0.6)^{7-0}+(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{1})(0.4)^{1}(0.6)^{7-1}+(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{2})(0.4)^{2}(0.6)^{7-2}] \\\\  & =1-[(0.6)^{7}+7(0.4)(0.6)^{6}+21(0.4)^{2}(0.6)^{5}] \\\\  & =1-0.419\\,904 \\\\  & ≈0.580,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nrounded to $3$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186435654 :question/id #uuid "4aa4655e-20ee-52b5-8d5f-be71eb721eca" :question/math-academy-id "q-89402" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "22f0b3b1-6694-51fa-b8a9-943b0a524d0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.871" :db/id 17592186435635} {:answer/id #uuid "69c9acef-9d33-557c-bd83-45aa9da4aecf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.931" :db/id 17592186435639} {:answer/id #uuid "b7b21599-df3a-56c7-be2f-08eed20c971f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.738" :db/id 17592186435643} {:answer/id #uuid "c283cf27-9162-56a8-84b2-ce532ab362b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.893" :db/id 17592186435644} {:answer/id #uuid "f90a7844-0f0f-53a0-969b-4a261303ee14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.973" :db/id 17592186435646}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435639} :answer-field/id #uuid "7d0f991d-9f23-5d9c-9970-8ed3243602c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435649}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "An archer practices firing an arrow at a target $20$ times. Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times the arrow hits the bullseye. \n\nHere, we have the following information:\n\n- there are $n=20$ trials\n\n- the probability of hitting the bull's eye is $p=20%=0.2$\n\nSo, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(20,0.2).$ \n\nThe number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function\n\n$$\nP(X=x)=(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},\n$$\n\nwhere $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.\n\nSubstituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{20}{x})(0.2)^{x}(1-0.2)^{20-x} \\\\  & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{20}{x})(0.2)^{x}(0.8)^{20-x}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe want to find the probability that the archer hits the bullseye at least $2$ times. This corresponds to $P(X\\ge 2).$\n\nHowever, computing\n\n$$\nP(X\\ge 2)=P(X=2)+P(X=3)+…+P(X=20)\n$$\n\nwill involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X\\ge 2) & =1-P(X<2) \\\\  & =1-[P(X=0)+P(X=1)] \\\\  & =1-[(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{20}{0})(0.2)^{0}(0.8)^{20-0}+(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{20}{1})(0.2)^{1}(0.8)^{20-1}] \\\\  & =1-[(0.8)^{20}+20(0.2)(0.8)^{19}] \\\\  & =1-0.069\\,175 \\\\  & =0.931\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nrounded to $3$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186435655 :question/id #uuid "a1fbc871-5104-5d0c-b476-cd8414e81086" :question/math-academy-id "q-276107" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "66e78e4d-d3e6-5a87-a64a-a52faa941ce7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.456" :db/id 17592186435638}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435638} :answer-field/id #uuid "aeab778f-c7ec-5e9d-a3d3-497eb92a9d85" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186435650}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "An unfair coin has a $15%$ chance of landing on heads. This corresponds to $P(X\\ge 2).$\n\nHowever, computing\n\n$$\nP(X\\ge 2)=P(X=2)+P(X=3)+…+P(X=10)\n$$\n\nwill involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X\\ge 2) & =1-P(X<2) \\\\  & =1-[P(X=0)+P(X=1)] \\\\  & =1-[(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{10}{0})(0.15)^{0}(0.85)^{10-0}+(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{10}{1})(0.15)^{1}(0.85)^{10-1}] \\\\  & =1-[(0.85)^{10}+10(0.15)(0.85)^{9}] \\\\  & ≈1-0.544\\,300 \\\\  & ≈0.456,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nrounded to $3$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186048597} {:db/id 17592186050425} {:db/id 17592186050738} {:db/id 17592186051022} {:db/id 17592186050308 :topic/difficulty 0.8258457054646602 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428372 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. $\\mathbf{v}$ such that \n\n$$\nA \\mathbf{v} = \\lambda \\mathbf{v}\n$$\n\nfor some scalar $\\lambda \\in \\mathbb{R}.$ The scalar $\\lambda$ is called the **eigenvalue** corresponding to the eigenvector $\\mathbf{v}.$\n\nFor example, consider the matrix \n![](images/63/63e2c65a23a0680412a14084d543b6cc19c0529fd80863b09c99987d309eaa4f.svg) \nand the vector ![](images/b7/b7811b74d8d3075357925864b5be27f57b292dadca9c04d222954baa1e66ba2a.svg) Computing the product $A \\cdot \\mathbf{v},$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Av & =[\\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\\\ 2 & -1\\end{aligned}]\\cdot [\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ -2\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}-2 \\\\ 4\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =(-2)\\cdot [\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ -2\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =-2v.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe've discovered that $A {\\color{blue}\\mathbf{v}} = {\\color{red}-2} {\\color{blue}\\mathbf{v}}.$ Therefore,\n\n- the vector ![](images/13/13a28e543647ede7a88b30fb652bd7fba6c9adb8ee3142161a102de947ef2d2a.svg) is an *eigenvector* of $A,$ and\n\n- the scalar $\\color{red}\\lambda=-2$ is the *eigenvalue* corresponding to the eigenvector ${\\color{blue}\\mathbf{v}}.$\n\n**Caution:** Remember that an eigenvector must be a *non-zero* vector.
