#uuid "563feb69-65ee-57de-a416-0f33d12b88c6" :step/math-academy-id 31791 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167721}} {:db/id 17592186167721 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168108 :tutorial/content "You might be wondering where the geometric distribution gets its name. The answer is that the probability mass function forms a geometric sequence! \n\nSuppose that $X\\sim \\textrm{Geom}(p).$ Then, the probability mass function for this geometric distribution is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-p)^{x-1}p \\\\ f(x) & =p(1-p)^{x-1} \\\\ {{f(x)}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{x}} & ={{p}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}\\cdot ({{1-p}_{⏟}}_{r})^{x-1} \\\\ {a}_{x} & ={a}_{1}\\cdot {r}^{x-1}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we see that the probability mass function can be interpreted as a geometric sequence where the first term is $a_1=p,$ and the common ratio is $r=1-p.$\n\nMoreover, notice that $f(x)$ satisfies all the criteria to be a probability mass function, namely\n\n- $0 \\leq f(x) \\leq 1$ for all $x$ in $S$\n\n- $\\displaystyle \\sum\\limits_{x \\in S} f(x) = 1$\n\nCriterion 1 is clearly true because $0 \\leq p \\leq 1.$ \n\nTo show that criterion 2 is true, we simply need to calculate the sum of this infinite geometric series, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\sum }_{x\\in S}f(x) & ={\\sum }_{x=1}^{\\infty }p(1-p)^{x-1} \\\\  & =\\frac{p}{1-(1-p)} \\\\  & =\\frac{p}{p} \\\\  & =1\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, $f(x)$ is indeed a probability distribution." :tutorial/id #uuid "0ac9b8c4-e381-5d24-b7f2-6e0cf660a14a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5365 :tutorial/title "Showing That a Geometric Distribution Is a Probability Distribution"} :step/id #uuid "4eb95a11-d9d7-553d-a1ee-58106336ccf8" :step/math-academy-id 33495} {:db/id 17592186167762 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168131 :tutorial/content "A **Bernoulli trial** is a random experiment whose outcome can be interpreted as either \"success\" or \"failure.\" \n\nFor example, suppose we throw a die and define a \"success\" as the event of getting a six and a \"failure\" as getting any other number. Then, the throw of a die can be thought of as a Bernoulli trial with the following probabilities:\n\n$$\nP(\\textrm{six}) = \\dfrac16, \\qquad P(\\textrm{not six}) = \\dfrac56\n$$\n\nNow suppose that a fair die is repeatedly thrown *until* we get a six. What is the probability that we need to throw the die precisely ${\\color{blue}{3}}$ times to get our first six?\n\nFirst, notice that each throw of the die is a Bernoulli trial. And since we throw the die repeatedly until we get a six, we have a *sequence* of Bernoulli trials. \n\nLet $X$ be the number of times the die is thrown until we get a six. We wish to compute $P(X = {\\color{blue}{3}}).$ \n\nTo get our first six on the *third* throw, we need to throw \"not a six\" on the *first two* throws, followed by a \"six\" on the *final* throw. Assuming that each throw of the die is independent, by the multiplication law for independent events, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X=3) & =P(\\text{not six})\\cdot P(\\text{not six})\\cdot P(\\text{six}) \\\\  & =\\frac{5}{6}\\cdot \\frac{5}{6}\\cdot \\frac{1}{6} \\\\  & =\\frac{25}{216}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe random variable $X$ in this example follows a so-called **geometric distribution**. Let's now discuss geometric distributions a little more generally." :tutorial/id #uuid "3201acc8-7bbc-59e6-9a50-f9c5f19899e7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6168 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "8ed0465c-f38c-56a2-acbf-cf8b05298867" :step/math-academy-id 37401 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167664}} {:db/id 17592186167763 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168132 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ be the number of times a fair die is thrown until we get a six. Since we have a sequence of Bernoulli trials, each with a probability of success $p=\\dfrac16,$ the number of throws until the first six can be modeled as a geometric random variable, and we write\n\n$$\nX\\sim \\textrm{Geom}\\left(\\dfrac16\\right).\n$$\n\nTherefore, the probability of getting our first six on the $\\color{blue}3$rd roll is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X=3) & =f(3) \\\\  & ={(1-\\frac{1}{6})}^{3-1}\\cdot \\frac{1}{6} \\\\  & ={(\\frac{5}{6})}^{2}\\cdot \\frac{1}{6} \\\\  & =\\frac{25}{36}\\cdot \\frac{1}{6} \\\\  & =\\frac{25}{216}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhich agrees with our previous result." :tutorial/id #uuid "95415f67-f3f8-5c48-9178-812ddf3830e1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6169 :tutorial/title "Applying the Probability Mass Function of a Geometric Distribution"} :step/id #uuid "0fec3647-5057-5207-8619-9dd7001d1b85" :step/math-academy-id 37402 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167667}}] :activity/title "The Geometric Distribution" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186167045} {:db/id 17592186167762 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168131 :tutorial/content "A **Bernoulli trial** is a random experiment whose outcome can be interpreted as either \"success\" or \"failure.\" \n\nFor example, suppose we throw a die and define a \"success\" as the event of getting a six and a \"failure\" as getting any other number. And since we throw the die repeatedly until we get a six, we have a *sequence* of Bernoulli trials. \n\nLet $X$ be the number of times the die is thrown until we get a six. We wish to compute $P(X = {\\color{blue}{3}}).$ \n\nTo get our first six on the *third* throw, we need to throw \"not a six\" on the *first two* throws, followed by a \"six\" on the *final* throw. Assuming that each throw of the die is independent, by the multiplication law for independent events, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X=3) & =P(\\text{not six})\\cdot P(\\text{not six})\\cdot P(\\text{six}) \\\\  & =\\frac{5}{6}\\cdot \\frac{5}{6}\\cdot \\frac{1}{6} \\\\  & =\\frac{25}{216}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe random variable $X$ in this example follows a so-called **geometric distribution**. Let's now discuss geometric distributions a little more generally." :tutorial/id #uuid "3201acc8-7bbc-59e6-9a50-f9c5f19899e7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6168 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186168132 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ be the number of times a fair die is thrown until we get a six. write\n\n$$\nX\\sim \\textrm{Geom}\\left(\\dfrac16\\right).\n$$\n\nTherefore, the probability of getting our first six on the $\\color{blue}3$rd roll is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X=3) & =f(3) \\\\  & ={(1-\\frac{1}{6})}^{3-1}\\cdot \\frac{1}{6} \\\\  & ={(\\frac{5}{6})}^{2}\\cdot \\frac{1}{6} \\\\  & =\\frac{25}{36}\\cdot \\frac{1}{6} \\\\  & =\\frac{25}{216}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhich agrees with our previous result." :tutorial/id #uuid "95415f67-f3f8-5c48-9178-812ddf3830e1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6169 :tutorial/title "Applying the Probability Mass Function of a Geometric Distribution"} For that reason, it's often helpful to plot the function when determining its range.\n\nFor example, consider the linear function\n\n$$\nf(x) =3-2x\n$$\n\nwhere $x$ is any real number. What is the range of $f(x)$?\n\nSince this is a linear function, we only need two points to plot it. For example:\n\n- When $x=0$, we have $y=3$. This gives the point $(0,3)$.\n- When $x=1$, we have $y=1$. This gives the point $(1,1)$.\n\nPlotting these two points and connecting them, we obtain the following diagram.\n\n![](images/51/5124e487118191ae40248d4488450d065fe71712f709ac62321d749ac17b0127.png)\n\nNotice that the graph $y=f(x)$ will cover all possible $y$-values, so the range of the function is\n\n$$\n-\\infty < y < \\infty\n$$\n\nUsing interval notation, we can also write the range as $(-\\infty, \\infty)$.\n\nLet's now look at an example of a linear function with a restricted domain." Let's define a transformation $\\mathbf T$ as\n\n$$\nx=r\\cos\\theta, \\qquad y = r\\sin\\theta.\n$$\n\nThe preimage of $D$ under the action of $\\mathbf T$ is the rectangular region $\\Delta,$ given by \n\n$$\n\\Delta = \\big\\{ (r,\\theta) \\: : \\: 1 \\leq r \\leq 2, \\: 0 \\leq \\theta \\leq 2\\pi \\big\\}.\n$$\n\nThe region $D$ and its preimage $\\Delta$ are shown \n\n$$\n\\iint\\limits_{D} f(x,y) \\ \\mathrm d A = \\iint\\limits_{\\Delta} \\ f(r\\cos\\theta, r\\sin\\theta) \\:  r \\ \\mathrm d r \\mathrm d \\theta.\n$$\n\nTherefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\\,dA & ={∬}_{Δ}\\sqrt{(r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta )^{2}+(r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta )^{2}}\\,r\\,\\text{d}r\\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }{\\int }_{1}^{2}\\sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta )}\\,r\\,dr\\,d\\theta  \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }{\\int }_{1}^{2}\\sqrt{{r}^{2}}\\cdot r\\,dr\\,d\\theta  \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }{\\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\\,dr\\,d\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nEvaluating this integral, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }{\\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\\,dr\\,d\\theta  & ={\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }d\\theta {\\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}\\,dr \\\\  & =2\\pi {\\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\\,dr \\\\  & =2\\pi \\cdot {[\\frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}]}_{1}^{2} \\\\  & =\\frac{2}{3}\\pi \\cdot [{2}^{3}-{1}^{3}] \\\\  & =\\frac{2}{3}\\pi \\cdot 7 \\\\  & =\\frac{14\\pi }{3}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we conclude that\n\n$$\n\\iint\\limits_{D}{{\\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\\,\\mathrm d A}} = \\dfrac{14\\pi}{3}.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "26614628-ce8b-5afe-ac90-b277c7c0f887" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4466 the region enclosed by the curve $x^2+(y-2)^2=4$ and the line $y=2,$ as shown below.\n\n![](images/df/dffcd94cc96c33d173704a63cb03fb0f0098bc67d6c66a855c16f59694bde8e1.png)\n\nThis region represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at $(0,2).$\n\nFirst, we recall the usual transformations from polar to Cartesian coordinates:\n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}x=r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  \\\\ y=r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nLet's now use the above formulas to write the functions that bound our region in polar coordinates:\n\n- For $x^2+(y-2)^2 = 4,$  we obtain \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2} & =4 \\\\ (r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta )^{2}+(r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta -2)^{2} & =4 \\\\ ({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta -4r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta +4 & =4 \\\\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta )-4r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & =0 \\\\ {r}^{2}-4r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & =0 \\\\ r(r-4\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ) & =0.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \nSince $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r = 4\\sin\\theta.$\n\n- For $y=2,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y & =2 \\\\ r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & =2 \\\\ r & =\\frac{2}{\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta } \\\\ r & =2\\operatorname{csc}⁡\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\\theta.$ \n\nFirst of all, note that if we draw an arrow through the region from the origin, it enters the region via the curve $r=2\\csc\\theta$ and exits via $r=4\\sin\\theta \\mathbin{:}$  \n\n![](images/b0/b09ab4e4e08dfb056964947dc866b965940b761d70c945faf001446c1df7869f.png)\n\nSecondly, our curves intersect at the points $(-2,2)$ and $(2,2).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\\theta=\\dfrac{\\pi}{4}$ and $\\theta=\\dfrac{3\\pi}{4},$ as depicted below.  \n\n![](images/6a/6a132d5f8c58ce60c794595ee80c57c5b9b02e630004808cd53a7677efd022e7.png)\n\nTherefore, in polar coordinates $(r, \\theta),$ the region can be expressed as follows:\n\n$$\n\\Delta = \\Big\\{ (r,\\theta) \\: : \\: 2\\csc\\theta \\leq r \\leq 4\\sin\\theta, \\: \\dfrac{\\pi}{4} \\leq \\theta \\leq \\dfrac{3\\pi}{4} \\Big\\}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid 17592186158487 :tutorial/content "Let's get some more practice at expressing regions in polar coordinates. \n\nConsider the region enclosed by the curve $x^2+(y-2)^2=4$ and the line $y=2,$ as shown below.\n\n![](images/df/dffcd94cc96c33d173704a63cb03fb0f0098bc67d6c66a855c16f59694bde8e1.png)\n\nThis region represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at $(0,2).$\n\nFirst, we recall the usual transformations from polar to Cartesian coordinates:\n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}x=r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  \\\\ y=r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nLet's now use the above formulas to write the functions that bound our region in polar coordinates:\n\n- For $x^2+(y-2)^2 = 4,$  we obtain \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2} & =4 \\\\ (r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta )^{2}+(r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta -2)^{2} & =4 \\\\ ({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta -4r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta +4 & =4 \\\\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta )-4r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & =0 \\\\ {r}^{2}-4r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & =0 \\\\ r(r-4\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ) & =0.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \nSince $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r = 4\\sin\\theta.$\n\n- For $y=2,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y & =2 \\\\ r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & =2 \\\\ r & =\\frac{2}{\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta } \\\\ r & =2\\operatorname{csc}⁡\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\\theta.$ \n\nFirst of all, note that if we draw an arrow through the region from the origin, it enters the region via the curve $r=2\\csc\\theta$ and exits via $r=4\\sin\\theta \\mathbin{:}$  \n\n![](images/b0/b09ab4e4e08dfb056964947dc866b965940b761d70c945faf001446c1df7869f.png)\n\nSecondly, our curves intersect at the points $(-2,2)$ and $(2,2).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\\theta=\\dfrac{\\pi}{4}$ and $\\theta=\\dfrac{3\\pi}{4},$ as depicted below.  \n\n![](images/6a/6a132d5f8c58ce60c794595ee80c57c5b9b02e630004808cd53a7677efd022e7.png)\n\nTherefore, in polar coordinates $(r, \\theta),$ the region can be expressed as follows:\n\n$$\n\\Delta = \\Big\\{ (r,\\theta) \\: : \\: 2\\csc\\theta \\leq r \\leq 4\\sin\\theta, \\: \\dfrac{\\pi}{4} \\leq \\theta \\leq \\dfrac{3\\pi}{4} \\Big\\}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form\n\n$$\n{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\\text{ }f(r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta )\\,r\\text{ }drd\\theta .\n$$\n\nNotice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at $(0,1).$ \n\nCartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:\n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}x=r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  \\\\ y=r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWith that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.\n\n- For ${x}^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=1,$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y-1)^{2} & =1 \\\\ (r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta )^{2}+(r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta -1)^{2} & =1 \\\\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta -2r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta +1 & =1 \\\\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta )-2r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & =0 \\\\ {r}^{2}-2r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & =0 \\\\ r(r-2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ) & =0.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \nSince $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta .$\n\n- For $y=1,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y & =1 \\\\ r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & =1 \\\\ r & =\\frac{1}{\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta } \\\\ r & =\\operatorname{csc}⁡\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let's find the limits for the parameter $\\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(-1,1).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\\theta =\\frac{\\pi }{2}$ and $\\theta =\\frac{3\\pi }{4},$ as depicted below.  \n\n![](images/1b/1b83e2674bba4bd6c326083f8c94496b5288de23575dc63a92b9a660eba69f67.png)\n\nAs a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\\theta )$ as \n\n$$\nΔ=\\{(r,\\theta )\\,:\\,\\operatorname{csc}⁡\\theta \\le r\\le 2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ,\\,\\frac{\\pi }{2}\\le \\theta \\le \\frac{3\\pi }{4}\\}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\\frac{4y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\\frac{4r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta }\\,r\\,\\text{d}r\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & ={\\int }_{\\pi /2}^{3\\pi /4}{\\int }_{\\operatorname{csc}⁡\\theta }^{2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta }4\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\,\\text{d}r\\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & ={\\int }_{\\pi /2}^{3\\pi /4}4\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta {\\int }_{\\operatorname{csc}⁡\\theta }^{2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta }\\,\\text{d}r\\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & ={\\int }_{\\pi /2}^{3\\pi /4}4\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta [r]_{\\operatorname{csc}⁡\\theta }^{2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta }\\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & ={\\int }_{\\pi /2}^{3\\pi /4}4\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta (2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta -\\operatorname{csc}⁡\\theta )\\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & =4{\\int }_{\\pi /2}^{3\\pi /4}(2{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta -1)\\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & =-4{\\int }_{\\pi /2}^{3\\pi /4}\\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\\theta )\\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & =-2[\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\\theta )]_{\\pi /2}^{3\\pi /4} \\\\  & =-2[\\operatorname{sin}⁡(\\frac{3\\pi }{2})-\\operatorname{sin}⁡(\\pi )] \\\\  & =2.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "c4072710-5fb0-565b-81f2-33d2fc972335" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436647}} "q-96589" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?\n\nSelect all that apply.\n\n- **I.** If $A$ is *any*  $n\\times n$ matrix, then ${A}^{2}$ is always symmetric.\n\n- **II.** The product of two $n\\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric.\n\n- **III.** If $A$ is a symmetric matrix, then ${A}^{-1}$ is always symmetric (if it exists)." :question/worked-solution "A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:\n\n$$\nA={A}^{T}\n$$\n\nEquivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.\n\nWith that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.\n\n- Statement I is false. As a counterexample, consider the matrix \n\n$\\,$ $A=[\\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\\\ 1 & 0\\end{aligned}].$\n\nHowever, ${A}^{2}$ is not symmetric:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\\\ 1 & 0\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\\\ 1 & 0\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\\\ 1 & -1\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Statement II is false. As a counterexample, consider the symmetric matrices \n\n$\\,$ $A=[\\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 0\\end{aligned}]\\,$ and $\\,B=[\\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}].$ \n\nHowever, their product is not symmetric:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}AB & =[\\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 0\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any non-singular symmetric matrix $A,$ we have \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}({A}^{-1})^{T} & =({A}^{T})^{-1} \\\\  & ={A}^{-1}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"III :question/worked-solution "Since $A$ is a $5\\times 5$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:\n\n$A$ is invertible $\\,⇔\\,{\\,\\begin{aligned} & \\text{Col}(A)={R}^{5} \\\\  & \\text{dim(Col}(A))=5=\\text{rank}(A) \\\\  & \\text{Null}(A)={0} \\\\  & \\text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\\text{nullity}(A)\\end{aligned}$\n\nAlso, according to the rank-nullity theorem, if $A$ is a matrix with $n$ columns, then \n\n$$\n\\text{rank}(A)+\\text{nullity}(A)=n.\n$$\n\nWith that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.\n\n- Statement I is true. Since $A$ has $n=5$ columns and $1$ of them is a non-pivot one, it follows that    \n\n$$\n\\text{dim(Col}(A))=5-1=4\\ne 5.\n$$\n\n Thus, according to the invertible matrix theorem $A$ is  **not** an invertible matrix.\n\n- Statement II is false. Since $\\text{dim(Col}(A))=\\text{rank}(A)=4$,  then $\\text{Col}(A)$ is a $4$-dimensional subspace of ${R}^{5}.$\n\n- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $n=5$, according to  the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{rank}(A)+\\text{nullity}(A) & =n \\\\ 4+\\text{nullity}(A) & =5 \\\\ \\text{nullity}(A) & =5-4 \\\\  & =1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I and III only.\""} {:db/id 17592186348222 :question/id #uuid "251cb9e2-c851-5082-b166-e39206cbabf3" :question/math-academy-id "q-79420" [{:db/id 17592186184937 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185320 :tutorial/content "When we reduce a matrix to row echelon form, the number of *pivot* columns plus the number of *non-pivot* columns always equals the total number of columns of the matrix. \n\nBy translating this into the language of vector spaces, we get the **rank-nullity theorem**. The rank-nullity theorem relates the rank of a matrix to the dimension of its null space:\n\n> *Let $A$ be a matrix (not necessarily square) with $n$ columns. Then,*\n> \n> \n> $$\n> \\textrm{dim(Col}(A)) + \\textrm{dim(Null}(A)) = \\textrm{dim}(\\mathbb{R}^n),\n> $$\n> \n> \n> *or, equivalently,*\n> \n> \n> $$\n> \\textrm{rank}(A) + \\textrm{nullity}(A) = n.\n> $$\n\nFor example, suppose that for some matrix $A,$ we have\n\n$$\n[\\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\\\ {x}_{2} \\\\ 2{x}_{3} \\\\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{3}\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\nWe can use the rank-nullity theorem to calculate $\\textrm{rank}(A).$\n\nIn this case, we must have $n=4,$ since this is the number of components in each of the vectors of the null space. \n\nAlso, we must have $\\textrm{nullity}(A)=2,$ since \n\n$$\n[\\begin{aligned}-2 \\\\ 1 \\\\ 0 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\nTherefore, using the rank-nullity theorem, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{rank}(A)+\\text{nullity}(A) & =n \\\\ \\text{rank}(A)+2 & =4 \\\\ \\text{rank}(A) & =4-2 \\\\  & =2.\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid [17592186046658 1007 "Mathematics for Machine Learning" 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.\nThis course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.\nOn completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.\nStudents then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.\nAs part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.\nStudents will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.\nThe course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.\nA solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.\nStudents also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.\nStudents work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.\nOn the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.\nStudents extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.\nThe course concludes with parametric inference, focusing on point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals, which form the statistical foundation for many machine learning methods." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1012 145 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I develops the core mathematical structures and analytical tools used throughout theoretical and applied physics. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.\nStudents learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.\nStudents then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.\nThe course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.\nThe course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.\nStudents then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.\nThe final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating strings, mechanical systems, and electromagnetic circuits." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1012 154 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1013 "PS1" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1014 #uuid The answer is that the probability mass function forms a geometric sequence! \n\nSuppose that $X\\sim \\textrm{Geom}(p).$ Then, the probability mass function for this geometric distribution is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-p)^{x-1}p \\\\ f(x) & =p(1-p)^{x-1} \\\\ {{f(x)}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{x}} & ={{p}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}\\cdot ({{1-p}_{⏟}}_{r})^{x-1} \\\\ {a}_{x} & ={a}_{1}\\cdot {r}^{x-1}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we see that the probability mass function can be interpreted as a geometric sequence where the first term is $a_1=p,$ and the common ratio is $r=1-p.$\n\nMoreover, notice that $f(x)$ satisfies all the criteria to be a probability mass function, namely\n\n- $0 \\leq f(x) \\leq 1$ for all $x$ in $S$\n\n- $\\displaystyle \\sum\\limits_{x \\in S} f(x) = 1$\n\nCriterion 1 is clearly true because $0 \\leq p \\leq 1.$ \n\nTo show that criterion 2 is true, we simply need to calculate the sum of this infinite geometric series, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\sum }_{x\\in S}f(x) & ={\\sum }_{x=1}^{\\infty }p(1-p)^{x-1} \\\\  & =\\frac{p}{1-(1-p)} \\\\  & =\\frac{p}{p} \\\\  & =1\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, $f(x)$ is indeed a probability distribution." 17592186045417] [17592186168108 1065 5365 17592186045417] [17592186168108 1066 #uuid "0ac9b8c4-e381-5d24-b7f2-6e0cf660a14a" 17592186045417] [17592186168108 1067 "Showing That a Geometric Distribution Is a Probability Distribution" 17592186045417] [17592186168131 1064 "A **Bernoulli trial** is a random experiment whose outcome can be interpreted as either \"success\" or \"failure.\" \n\nFor example, suppose we throw a die and define a \"success\" as the event of getting a six and a \"failure\" as getting any other number.
